sectionTitle: The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere

specStatements.text: For 200 million years, the proportions of different gases in the atmosphere have been much the same as they are today:
small proportions of various other gases, including carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases.

Theories about what was in the Earth’s early atmosphere and how the atmosphere was formed have changed and developed over time. Evidence for the early atmosphere is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years.

One theory suggests that during the first billion years of the Earth’s existence there was intense volcanic activity that released gases that formed the early atmosphere and water vapour that condensed to form the oceans. At the start of this period the Earth’s atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today, consisting of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
Volcanoes also produced nitrogen which gradually built up in the atmosphere and there may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia.

When the oceans formed carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated producing sediments, reducing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. No knowledge of other theories is required.
Students should be able to, given appropriate information, interpret evidence and evaluate different theories about the Earth’s early atmosphere.
Algae and plants produced the oxygen that is now in the atmosphere by photosynthesis, which can be represented by the equation:

Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago and soon after this oxygen appeared in the atmosphere. Over the next billion years plants evolved and the percentage of oxygen gradually increased to a level that enabled animals to evolve.
Algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere by photosynthesis.
Carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon.
describe the main changes in the atmosphere over time and some of the likely causes of these changes
describe and explain the formation of deposits of limestone, coal, crude oil and natural gas.

scopeNotes.statement: No knowledge of other theories is required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the theory named in the specification is taught: intense volcanic activity in the first billion years releasing gases and water vapour, an early atmosphere mainly of carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen, volcanic nitrogen building up, possible small proportions of methane and ammonia, and carbon dioxide dissolving in the new oceans so that carbonates were precipitated as sediments. No rival account of the origin of the atmosphere or of the oceans is introduced, named or examined. The evaluation item (q12) asks students to weigh the strength of the evidence for the specified theory, not to compare it with an alternative theory they have not been taught.

concepts.definition: For the last 200 million years the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere have been much the same as they are today. The atmosphere has therefore been broadly stable over that period, but was very different before it.
Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths (approximately 80%) of the atmosphere. It is the most abundant gas in the air today.
Oxygen makes up about one-fifth (approximately 20%) of the atmosphere. It is the second most abundant gas in the air today.

The remainder of the atmosphere is made up of small proportions of various other gases, including carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases. Together these account for only a small proportion of the air.

concepts.term: Why evidence for the early atmosphere is limited
concepts.definition: Evidence for the Earth's early atmosphere is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years. Scientists cannot sample an atmosphere that existed billions of years ago, so conclusions rest on indirect evidence.

Theories about what was in the Earth's early atmosphere and how the atmosphere was formed have changed and developed over time. A theory is the current best explanation of the available evidence and is revised as new evidence is found.
One theory suggests that during the first billion years of the Earth's existence there was intense volcanic activity that released the gases which formed the early atmosphere.
The same volcanic activity released water vapour, which condensed to form the oceans as the Earth cooled.
At the start of this period the Earth's atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today, consisting of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
Volcanoes also produced nitrogen, which gradually built up in the atmosphere. Because nitrogen is unreactive it was not readily removed, so its proportion increased over time.
There may also have been small proportions of methane and ammonia in the early atmosphere.
When the oceans formed, carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated, producing sediments. This reduced the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

concepts.term: Evaluating theories about the early atmosphere
concepts.definition: Given appropriate information, students should be able to interpret evidence and evaluate different theories about the Earth's early atmosphere, judging how far the evidence supports a claim and where its limitations lie.

Algae and plants produced the oxygen that is now in the atmosphere by photosynthesis, which can be represented by the equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, that is, carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.

Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago and soon after this oxygen appeared in the atmosphere. Over the next billion years plants evolved and the percentage of oxygen gradually increased to a level that enabled animals to evolve.
Algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere by photosynthesis, because the reaction uses carbon dioxide as a reactant.

concepts.term: Carbon locked into rocks and fuels
concepts.definition: Carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon. Carbon taken from the atmosphere by living organisms was buried and retained in these deposits.

Limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms, which are made of calcium carbonate. These deposits built up on the sea bed and were buried and compressed, locking carbon into the rock.

Coal is a sedimentary rock formed from thick deposits of plant material. The plants were buried by sediment and, over millions of years, heat and pressure in the absence of oxygen converted the deposits to coal.

concepts.term: Formation of crude oil and natural gas
concepts.definition: Crude oil and natural gas were formed from the remains of plankton (marine organisms) that were buried in mud on the sea bed and changed over millions of years by heat and pressure in the absence of oxygen.

concepts.term: Main changes in the atmosphere over time
concepts.definition: The main changes are a large decrease in carbon dioxide and an increase in oxygen. Carbon dioxide fell because it dissolved in the oceans and was precipitated as carbonates, was used in photosynthesis, and was locked into sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels; oxygen rose because algae and then plants photosynthesised.

misconceptions.question: Which gas makes up about four-fifths of the air?
misconceptions.correct: Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths (approximately 80%) of the atmosphere; oxygen makes up about one-fifth (approximately 20%).
misconceptions.misconception: Oxygen is the main gas in the air, because it is the gas we need, so it must be about 80%.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxygen is the gas students hear about constantly – in breathing, burning and rusting – so importance is mistaken for abundance. Nitrogen is rarely mentioned because it is unreactive.
misconceptions.correction: Importance is not the same as abundance. Nitrogen is about 80% of the air and oxygen about 20%; oxygen matters to us because of what it does, not because there is a lot of it.

misconceptions.question: Roughly what proportion of today's atmosphere is carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide is one of the various other gases present in only small proportions.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide must be a big part of the air, because everyone talks about how much of it there is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon dioxide dominates discussion of climate change and of respiration, and pie charts in textbooks often exaggerate its slice so it can be seen at all.
misconceptions.correction: Nitrogen (about 80%) and oxygen (about 20%) account for nearly all of the air. Carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases together make up only the small remaining proportion.

misconceptions.question: Did the Earth's early atmosphere contain much oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: One theory suggests the early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
misconceptions.misconception: There must always have been oxygen in the air, otherwise nothing could have survived.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason backwards from the present: because life needs oxygen now, they assume oxygen has always been there, and they do not picture a world without living things.
misconceptions.correction: The oxygen came later. It was produced by algae from about 2.7 billion years ago and then by plants; at the start there was little or no oxygen gas, which is why only organisms that did not need oxygen could exist.

misconceptions.question: For how long have the proportions of gases in the atmosphere been much the same as today?
misconceptions.correct: For 200 million years the proportions have been much the same as they are today.
misconceptions.misconception: The air has been the same for the whole 4.6 billion years since the Earth formed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 4.6 billion years is the figure students meet most often, so it is attached to every fact about the Earth. The idea that air itself has a history is unfamiliar.
misconceptions.correction: 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth and the reason evidence about the early atmosphere is limited. The present proportions have only held for the last 200 million years.

misconceptions.question: Why can scientists not be certain what the early atmosphere contained?
misconceptions.correct: Evidence for the early atmosphere is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years.
misconceptions.misconception: Scientists must know exactly what the early atmosphere was, because they can measure these things now.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students trust that modern instruments can measure anything, and do not distinguish between measuring something that exists now and reconstructing something that vanished billions of years ago.
misconceptions.correction: No sample of the early atmosphere survives. Because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years the evidence is limited and indirect, so ideas about the early atmosphere remain theories.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean that theories about the early atmosphere have changed over time?
misconceptions.correct: Theories have changed and developed over time as new evidence has been gathered and interpreted.
misconceptions.misconception: If the theory keeps changing, then scientists were careless before and science cannot be trusted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect science to deliver fixed facts, so revision looks like failure rather than the normal way scientific explanations improve.
misconceptions.correction: Changing a theory when new evidence appears is exactly how science is supposed to work. Earlier scientists were reasoning from the evidence they had; more evidence produced a better explanation.

misconceptions.question: Where did the water in the oceans come from?
misconceptions.correct: Volcanic activity released water vapour which condensed to form the oceans.
misconceptions.misconception: The water in the oceans was made by plants, because photosynthesis produces water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Water appears in both the photosynthesis and respiration equations, so students reach for a biological source for water instead of a volcanic one.
misconceptions.correction: In the photosynthesis equation water is a reactant, not a product. The ocean water came from water vapour released by intense volcanic activity, which condensed as the Earth cooled.

misconceptions.question: Where did the nitrogen in the atmosphere come from?
misconceptions.correct: Volcanoes produced nitrogen which gradually built up in the atmosphere.
misconceptions.misconception: Living things made the nitrogen, in the same way that plants made the oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Having learned that algae and plants produced the oxygen, students apply the same explanation to the other major gas.
misconceptions.correction: Nitrogen came from volcanoes and built up gradually because it is unreactive and is not readily removed. Only the oxygen is attributed to algae and plants.

misconceptions.question: How much of the air is made up of the noble gases?
misconceptions.correct: The noble gases are among the various other gases present in only small proportions.
misconceptions.misconception: The noble gases are a whole group of the periodic table, so together they must make up a large share of the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A group of eight elements sounds substantial, and argon is often singled out in diagrams of the air, which makes it look more abundant than it is.
misconceptions.correction: The number of elements in a group says nothing about their abundance. The noble gases in the air are part of the small proportion of other gases left after about 80% nitrogen and about 20% oxygen.

misconceptions.question: What happened about 2.7 billion years ago?
misconceptions.correct: Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago, and soon after this oxygen appeared in the atmosphere.
misconceptions.misconception: About 2.7 billion years ago the atmosphere reached the composition it has today.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students collect the dates in this topic without attaching each one to its event, so 2.7 billion years is used as a general 'the air became normal' marker.
misconceptions.correction: 2.7 billion years ago is when algae first produced oxygen. The percentage of oxygen then rose gradually over the next billion years; the present proportions have only held for the last 200 million years.

misconceptions.question: Which came first, algae or plants?
misconceptions.correct: Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago; over the next billion years plants evolved.
misconceptions.misconception: Plants came first and algae evolved from them later on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Plants are the familiar photosynthesising organisms, so students assume they were the original ones and treat algae as a minor afterthought.
misconceptions.correction: Algae were first, producing oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago. Plants evolved over the following billion years, and the percentage of oxygen increased to a level that enabled animals to evolve.

misconceptions.question: What does photosynthesis do to the carbon dioxide in the air?
misconceptions.correct: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide, so algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
misconceptions.misconception: Photosynthesis gives out carbon dioxide, because that is what living things breathe out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Photosynthesis and respiration have the same substances on opposite sides of the equation, and students who have memorised only the substances lose track of which side each is on.
misconceptions.correction: In photosynthesis carbon dioxide and water are the reactants and glucose and oxygen the products: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. Photosynthesis therefore removes carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.

misconceptions.question: Which process decreased the carbon dioxide in the early atmosphere?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide decreased through dissolving in the oceans and being precipitated as carbonates, through photosynthesis, and through the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
misconceptions.misconception: Respiration is what took the carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Respiration is the process students associate most strongly with carbon dioxide, and they do not check the direction: respiration releases carbon dioxide, it does not remove it.
misconceptions.correction: Respiration releases carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide was removed by dissolving in the oceans and precipitating as carbonates, by photosynthesis, and by burial as sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.

misconceptions.question: Evidence about the early atmosphere is limited. What follows from that?
misconceptions.correct: Limited evidence means theories are provisional, but they are still judged on how well the available evidence supports them.
misconceptions.misconception: There is no real evidence at all, so one guess about the early atmosphere is as good as another.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'limited' as 'none', and conclude that if certainty is impossible then all ideas are equal and evaluation is pointless.
misconceptions.correction: Limited evidence is not zero evidence. Evidence such as the composition of the atmospheres of Mars and Venus, and the carbonate sediments in ancient rocks, supports some explanations better than others, so theories can still be evaluated.

misconceptions.question: What was the main gas in the Earth's early atmosphere?
misconceptions.correct: One theory suggests the early atmosphere consisted of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
misconceptions.misconception: The early atmosphere must have been mainly nitrogen and oxygen, because that is what air is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat today's composition as what 'air' means by definition, and so project about 80% nitrogen and about 20% oxygen back to the beginning.
misconceptions.correction: The early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide. Nitrogen built up gradually from volcanic activity and oxygen only appeared once algae began to photosynthesise about 2.7 billion years ago.

misconceptions.question: Mars and Venus have carbon dioxide atmospheres. What does that show?
misconceptions.correct: The Earth's early atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today, consisting of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
misconceptions.misconception: Because Mars and Venus have carbon dioxide atmospheres, we know for certain the early Earth did too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A comparison that supports an idea is easily read as proof of it, especially when the specification's wording 'may have been' is skimmed over.
misconceptions.correction: Mars and Venus provide supporting evidence, not proof. They are different planets that may have developed differently, so the comparison makes the theory plausible without confirming it.

misconceptions.question: Were the Earth's oceans and its present gases there from the start?
misconceptions.correct: The gases of the early atmosphere were released by volcanic activity, and the oceans formed when volcanic water vapour condensed.
misconceptions.misconception: The oceans and the gases were all there from the moment the Earth formed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the Earth forming complete, like a finished model, rather than as a body whose surface and atmosphere developed over the first billion years.
misconceptions.correction: During the first billion years intense volcanic activity released the gases that formed the early atmosphere, along with the water vapour that condensed to form the oceans.

misconceptions.question: Where did the oxygen in the atmosphere come from?
misconceptions.correct: Algae and plants produced the oxygen that is now in the atmosphere by photosynthesis.
misconceptions.misconception: Sunlight split the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, and that is where the oxygen came from.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know sunlight is involved in producing oxygen and know carbon dioxide contains oxygen, and combine the two into a purely physical process with no organisms in it.
misconceptions.correction: The oxygen was produced by living organisms: algae from about 2.7 billion years ago, and later plants, by photosynthesis, 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2.

misconceptions.question: Did volcanoes produce all the gases in today's atmosphere?
misconceptions.correct: Volcanoes released the gases of the early atmosphere, including carbon dioxide and nitrogen; the oxygen came from photosynthesis by algae and plants.
misconceptions.misconception: Volcanoes released every gas in the air, so the oxygen came from volcanoes too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Once students learn that volcanic activity formed the early atmosphere, they extend it to the whole of the modern atmosphere and overlook the biological origin of oxygen.
misconceptions.correction: Volcanic gases account for the carbon dioxide, the nitrogen and possibly the methane and ammonia. The oxygen now in the atmosphere was produced by algae and plants through photosynthesis.

misconceptions.question: Why could animals only evolve when they did?
misconceptions.correct: Over the billion years after algae appeared, plants evolved and the percentage of oxygen gradually increased to a level that enabled animals to evolve.
misconceptions.misconception: Animals were around before there was much oxygen, and the oxygen built up around them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of the fossil record as a story about animals, so animals are placed at the beginning rather than as latecomers who depended on oxygen already being present.
misconceptions.correction: Oxygen came first. Algae produced it from about 2.7 billion years ago and plants added to it over the next billion years, until the percentage of oxygen reached a level that enabled animals to evolve.

misconceptions.question: How are fossil fuels linked to the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide was decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon.
misconceptions.misconception: Fossil fuels only put carbon dioxide into the air, so they cannot have taken any out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet fossil fuels almost exclusively as something that is burned, so the formation of the fuel, which locked carbon away, is never considered.
misconceptions.correction: Two separate events. When fossil fuels formed, carbon taken from the air by living organisms was buried and locked away, decreasing carbon dioxide. Burning them now returns that carbon to the atmosphere.

misconceptions.question: What happened to the carbon dioxide that left the early atmosphere?
misconceptions.correct: It dissolved in the oceans and was precipitated as carbonate sediments, was used in photosynthesis, and was locked into sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
misconceptions.misconception: The carbon dioxide escaped from the Earth into space.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who cannot name a chemical sink for the gas reach for the only other destination they can picture, and gas escaping upwards feels intuitive.
misconceptions.correction: The carbon did not leave the planet; it moved into the oceans, into carbonate sediments, into sedimentary rocks such as limestone, and into fossil fuels. Each of these is a store of carbon on Earth.

misconceptions.question: Were limestone, coal, crude oil and natural gas all formed in the same way?
misconceptions.correct: Limestone formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms; coal from thick deposits of plant material; crude oil and natural gas from plankton buried in mud.
misconceptions.misconception: They are all buried remains, so it does not matter which organisms each one came from.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All four are taught together as carbon stores formed by burial over millions of years, and the shared process makes the different starting materials feel interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: The starting material is the point of difference. Shells and skeletons give limestone, thick plant deposits give coal, and plankton buried in mud give crude oil and natural gas.

misconceptions.question: How did limestone form?
misconceptions.correct: Limestone formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms, which are made of calcium carbonate.
misconceptions.misconception: Limestone is made from volcanic material that settled and hardened into rock.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Volcanic activity dominates the early part of this topic, so students use it to explain rock formation generally and do not separate sedimentary rock from igneous rock.
misconceptions.correction: Limestone is a sedimentary rock. It formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms deposited on the sea bed, which is how carbon from the atmosphere became locked into rock.

misconceptions.question: What was crude oil formed from?
misconceptions.correct: Crude oil and natural gas were formed from plankton, that is, marine organisms buried in mud.
misconceptions.misconception: Crude oil was formed from the remains of dinosaurs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'fossil fuel' plus popular images of dinosaur-era swamps produce a memorable but wrong story that students rarely question.
misconceptions.correction: Crude oil and natural gas formed from plankton – microscopic marine organisms – buried in mud on the sea bed and altered over millions of years by heat and pressure.

misconceptions.question: What was coal formed from?
misconceptions.correct: Coal was formed from thick deposits of plant material.
misconceptions.misconception: Coal formed from the buried bodies of land animals.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Once oil has been attached to animal remains, coal is assumed to have an animal origin too, since both are fossil fuels formed by burial.
misconceptions.correction: Coal formed from thick deposits of plant material that were buried and compressed over millions of years, which is why coal is essentially carbon that plants had taken from the atmosphere.

misconceptions.question: Does the photosynthesis equation need to balance?
misconceptions.correct: The equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, which balances: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen atoms on each side.
misconceptions.misconception: As long as the right substances are on the right sides, the numbers in front do not really matter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat the equation as a word summary written in symbols, so the big numbers look decorative rather than as a statement that atoms are conserved.
misconceptions.correction: Atoms are not created or destroyed, so the numbers must make each element balance. 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 3O2 is wrong because oxygen atoms do not balance.

mcqs.stem: For roughly how long have the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere been much the same as they are today?

options.text: About 200 million years
options.rationale: The specification states that for 200 million years the proportions of the different gases have been much the same as they are today.

options.text: About 4.6 billion years
options.rationale: 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth, and students attach it to any question about the Earth's history.

options.text: About 2.7 billion years
options.rationale: 2.7 billion years ago is when algae first produced oxygen, not when the modern proportions were reached.

options.text: About one billion years
options.rationale: The first billion years is the period of intense volcanic activity, when the atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide, not like today's.

mcqs.stem: Which of these best describes the proportions of the two main gases in the atmosphere today?

options.text: About 80% oxygen and about 20% nitrogen
options.rationale: A student who judges abundance by importance puts oxygen first, because oxygen is the gas that living things need.

options.text: About 80% nitrogen, about 20% oxygen
options.rationale: Nitrogen is about four-fifths (approximately 80%) of the atmosphere and oxygen about one-fifth (approximately 20%).

options.text: About 80% nitrogen, 20% carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is the gas talked about most, so it is promoted into the second place that belongs to oxygen.

options.text: About 50% nitrogen and 50% oxygen gas
options.rationale: A student who remembers only that nitrogen and oxygen are the two main gases splits the air evenly between them.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases in the air today is correct?

options.text: Together they make up about one fifth.
options.rationale: One fifth is the proportion of oxygen; a student who overestimates carbon dioxide gives these gases oxygen's share.

options.text: Carbon dioxide alone makes up about 20%.
options.rationale: The prominence of carbon dioxide in discussions of climate change leads students to greatly overestimate how much is present.

options.text: Together they make up a small part.
options.rationale: The specification describes these as small proportions of various other gases, left after about 80% nitrogen and about 20% oxygen.

options.text: The noble gases make up about one fifth.
options.rationale: A whole group of the periodic table sounds substantial, so its combined abundance is overestimated.

mcqs.stem: Why is the evidence about the Earth's early atmosphere limited?

options.text: Instruments to measure it have not been built.
options.rationale: A student who trusts that modern instruments can measure anything blames the technology rather than the passage of time.

options.text: There is no evidence about it left at all.
options.rationale: 'Limited' is read as 'none', which would make evaluating theories impossible.

options.text: The early atmosphere had undetectable gases.
options.rationale: The gases proposed – carbon dioxide, nitrogen, methane, ammonia – are all easily detected; the problem is that no sample survives.

options.text: The time scale involved is 4.6 billion years.
options.rationale: The specification gives exactly this reason: evidence is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years.

mcqs.stem: Theories about the Earth's early atmosphere have changed and developed over time. What does this best show?

options.text: Explanations are revised when new evidence appears.
options.rationale: Theories are the current best explanation of the available evidence and develop as more evidence is gathered.

options.text: The earlier scientists were careless in their work.
options.rationale: Students who expect science to deliver fixed facts read revision as somebody's mistake.

options.text: Evidence about the early atmosphere is now complete.
options.rationale: Because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years the evidence remains limited, which is why theories are still being developed.

options.text: Scientific ideas about the past are never reliable.
options.rationale: The overreaction to changing theories: if ideas can change, a student concludes none of them count.

mcqs.stem: According to the theory in the specification, what was the Earth's atmosphere like at the start of its first billion years?

options.text: Oxygen, with little or no carbon dioxide
options.rationale: A student who assumes oxygen has always been present simply swaps the two gases round.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen
options.rationale: The specification states the atmosphere may have been like those of Mars and Venus today, mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.

options.text: Nitrogen, with little or no carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Today's composition is projected backwards, because nitrogen is what 'air' means to the student.

options.text: Methane, with a large amount of oxygen
options.rationale: Methane may have been present in small proportions only, and oxygen was scarce; both parts of this option are wrong.

mcqs.stem: Scientists use the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today as a model for the Earth's early atmosphere. Why?

options.text: They consist mainly of nitrogen and oxygen.
options.rationale: A student who thinks all atmospheres must resemble today's air describes Mars and Venus as though they were the Earth.

options.text: They have exactly the same atmosphere as us.
options.rationale: The comparison is read as identity rather than as similarity offered in support of a theory.

options.text: They consist mainly of carbon dioxide today.
options.rationale: The specification says the early Earth's atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus, mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen.

options.text: They have no atmosphere at all to compare.
options.rationale: Both planets do have atmospheres; a planet with none could tell us nothing about the early Earth.

mcqs.stem: According to the theory in the specification, how did the Earth's oceans form?

options.text: Water vapour from photosynthesis condensed.
options.rationale: Water appears in the photosynthesis equation, so a biological source is chosen; but there water is a reactant, not a product.

options.text: The oceans were there when Earth formed.
options.rationale: The Earth is pictured as forming complete, rather than developing its atmosphere and oceans over the first billion years.

options.text: Water vapour froze and then melted again.
options.rationale: The specification describes condensation of water vapour, not freezing; adding a freezing step is an invented mechanism.

options.text: Water vapour from volcanoes condensed.
options.rationale: Intense volcanic activity released water vapour, which condensed to form the oceans as the Earth cooled.

mcqs.stem: Where did the nitrogen in the Earth's atmosphere come from?

options.text: Volcanoes produced it and it built up slowly.
options.rationale: The specification states that volcanoes also produced nitrogen, which gradually built up in the atmosphere.

options.text: Algae produced it during photosynthesis.
options.rationale: The explanation given for oxygen is transferred to the other major gas of the modern atmosphere.

options.text: It was present when the Earth first formed.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the atmosphere came ready-made sees no need for a source for any gas.

options.text: It escaped from the oceans as they warmed.
options.rationale: The oceans formed from condensed volcanic water vapour; they are not the source of atmospheric nitrogen.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of gases may have been present in small proportions in the Earth's early atmosphere?

options.text: Methane and oxygen
options.rationale: Methane is remembered correctly, but oxygen is added by a student who assumes oxygen was always there.

options.text: Methane and ammonia
options.rationale: The specification states there may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia.

options.text: Ammonia and argon
options.rationale: Argon is imported from the list of gases in today's air, where the noble gases are a small proportion.

options.text: Hydrogen and helium
options.rationale: These are the gases of the Sun and giant planets; they are not the gases the specification names for the early Earth.

mcqs.stem: When the oceans formed, how was carbon dioxide removed from the atmosphere?

options.text: Sunlight broke it down into carbon and oxygen.
options.rationale: A physical mechanism is invented for a change that was chemical, and it also misattributes the origin of oxygen.

options.text: It was used up by animals during respiration.
options.rationale: Respiration is associated with carbon dioxide, but it releases the gas rather than removing it, and animals had not yet evolved.

options.text: It dissolved and carbonates were precipitated.
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated, producing sediments and reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide.

options.text: It reacted with the nitrogen to form nitrates.
options.rationale: Nitrogen is unreactive and built up in the atmosphere; no such reaction is part of the specified account.

mcqs.stem: A scientist argues that because Mars and Venus have atmospheres of mainly carbon dioxide, the Earth's early atmosphere was certainly the same. What is the main weakness of this argument?

options.text: Data sent back by space probes are never reliable.
options.rationale: Limited evidence is treated as worthless evidence, so the data are dismissed instead of being weighed.

options.text: Ideas about the distant past can never be tested.
options.rationale: A student who thinks changing theories mean unreliable science concludes that testing is impossible.

options.text: Carbon dioxide cannot be detected from far away.
options.rationale: The composition of planetary atmospheres can be determined remotely; the weakness lies in the inference, not the measurement.

options.text: Other planets may have developed in different ways.
options.rationale: The comparison supports the theory but does not confirm it; Mars and Venus are different planets with their own histories.

mcqs.stem: Which equation represents photosynthesis, as given in the specification?

options.rationale: This is the equation given in the specification, and it balances with 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side.
This is respiration. A student who has memorised the substances but not their sides writes the reaction backwards.
The substances are right but the equation does not balance: only 15 oxygen atoms appear on the right.
Halving the carbon dioxide leaves too few carbon and oxygen atoms on the left for the glucose formed.

mcqs.stem: Which process produced the oxygen that is now in the Earth's atmosphere?

options.text: Respiration by early algae and plants
options.rationale: Photosynthesis and respiration are confused, so the process that uses oxygen is credited with making it.

options.text: Photosynthesis by algae and plants
options.rationale: The specification states that algae and plants produced the oxygen now in the atmosphere by photosynthesis.

options.text: Volcanic activity on the early Earth
options.rationale: Volcanoes released carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water vapour, but the early atmosphere had little or no oxygen.

options.text: Condensation of the volcanic vapour
options.rationale: Condensation of water vapour formed the oceans; it produced liquid water, not oxygen gas.

mcqs.stem: About how long ago did algae first produce oxygen?

options.text: About 4.6 billion years ago
options.rationale: 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth, the figure a student reaches for by default.

options.text: About 200 million years ago
options.rationale: 200 million years is how long the modern proportions have held, a much later stage of the story.

options.text: About 2.7 billion years ago
options.rationale: The specification states that algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago.

options.text: About 1.5 million years ago
options.rationale: This is far too recent; animals had already evolved long before, which required oxygen to be present.

mcqs.stem: Which sequence matches the way the specification describes the rise of oxygen?

options.text: Plants evolved, then algae made oxygen, then animals
options.rationale: Plants are the familiar photosynthesisers, so a student places them before algae.

options.text: Animals evolved, then algae made oxygen, then plants
options.rationale: Animals are put first by a student who does not realise they depended on oxygen already being present.

options.text: Algae made oxygen, then animals evolved, then plants
options.rationale: This keeps algae first but places animals before the plants that added most of the oxygen they needed.

options.text: Algae made oxygen, then plants evolved, then animals
options.rationale: Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago, plants evolved over the next billion years, and the rising percentage of oxygen enabled animals to evolve.

mcqs.stem: What effect did the spread of algae and plants have on the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

options.text: It decreased, because photosynthesis uses it.
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is a reactant in photosynthesis, so algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide.

options.text: It increased, because photosynthesis makes it.
options.rationale: The photosynthesis equation is reversed, putting carbon dioxide among the products.

options.text: It decreased, because respiration removes it.
options.rationale: The right direction for the wrong reason: respiration releases carbon dioxide rather than removing it.

options.text: It stayed the same, as plants use no gases.
options.rationale: Photosynthesis is a gas exchange in both directions, so plants could not leave the atmosphere unchanged.

mcqs.stem: Apart from photosynthesis, what else decreased the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

options.text: Burning fossil fuels took it out of the air.
options.rationale: Fossil fuels are met only as something that is burned, so their formation as a carbon store is overlooked.

options.text: Carbon became locked in rocks and fossil fuels.
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon.

options.text: Carbon dioxide escaped from Earth into space.
options.rationale: With no chemical sink in mind, a student sends the gas upwards and off the planet.

options.text: Carbon dioxide was destroyed by the sunlight.
options.rationale: Sunlight is invoked as a general destroyer of gases; carbon dioxide was in fact transferred to oceans and rocks.

mcqs.stem: How were deposits of limestone formed?

options.text: From thick deposits of buried plant material
options.rationale: The starting materials for the different carbon stores are treated as interchangeable; plant deposits give coal.

options.text: From volcanic ash settling onto the sea bed
options.rationale: Volcanic activity dominates the early part of the topic, so it is used to explain rock formation in general.

options.text: From shells and skeletons of marine organisms
options.rationale: Limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from the calcium carbonate shells and skeletons of marine organisms deposited on the sea bed.

options.text: From plankton buried in mud on the sea bed
options.rationale: Plankton buried in mud gave crude oil and natural gas, not limestone.

mcqs.stem: Crude oil and natural gas were formed from the remains of which organisms?

options.text: Thick deposits of buried plant material
options.rationale: Coal's starting material is applied to oil, because all fossil fuels are assumed to form the same way.

options.text: Remains of dinosaurs buried in the rock
options.rationale: The popular image of oil coming from dinosaurs is memorable and is rarely questioned.

options.text: Carbonate sediments from the sea water
options.rationale: Precipitated carbonates produced limestone; they are not the origin of crude oil or natural gas.

options.text: Plankton buried in mud on the sea floor
options.rationale: Crude oil and natural gas formed from plankton, marine organisms buried in mud and altered over millions of years.

mcqs.stem: Coal is a sedimentary rock. What was it formed from?

options.text: Thick deposits of plant material
options.rationale: Coal formed from thick deposits of plant material that were buried and compressed over millions of years.

options.text: Plankton buried in sea-bed mud
options.rationale: Oil's starting material is applied to coal, since both are fossil fuels formed by burial.

options.text: Remains of buried land animals
options.rationale: Once oil is attached to animal remains, coal is given an animal origin too.

options.text: Precipitated carbonate sediment
options.rationale: Precipitated carbonates produced limestone, a rock that is not a fuel.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of changes describes how the Earth's atmosphere changed over most of its history?

options.text: Carbon dioxide rose and oxygen fell
options.rationale: A student who thinks the early atmosphere was oxygen-rich has to make oxygen fall over time.

options.text: Carbon dioxide fell and oxygen rose
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide was removed by the oceans, carbonate precipitation, photosynthesis and burial as rocks and fuels, while photosynthesis released oxygen.

options.text: Both carbon dioxide and oxygen rose
options.rationale: If volcanoes are credited with releasing every gas, both would increase together.

options.text: Both carbon dioxide and oxygen fell
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide did fall, but oxygen rose to the level that enabled animals to evolve.
